strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem framing: the paper quantifies the 'complexity cliff' in LLaVA-665K (90% of questions require ≤2 capabilities) and proposes explicitly controlling compositional complexity during VIT data generation, which is a sensible and underexplored angle.

The data generation pipeline is well-designed and documented: capability taxonomy from literature, structured Gemini prompting with explicit constraints, an independent quality/capability verification step, and iterative filtering; prompts are provided in the appendix.

Strong and diverse benchmark suite (8 benchmarks spanning OCR, perception, compositional reasoning), plus a meaningful set of ablations: unbalanced-k control (showing the balanced distribution is the key driver, 96.62% vs 98.83%), leave-one-out capability analysis, complexity-range ablation, and instruction-tuning-mix ratio study.

Compelling data-efficiency result: matching full-scale VIT with ~10% of the data budget, outperforming both a random subset and the ICONS selection baseline at equal data size, with consistent trends across data scales (Fig. 3).
Limitations are candidly discussed (closed-source model dependence, cost, restricted scope to vision-centric capabilities), and the authors commit to releasing the generated data.
weaknesses: Evaluation is limited to a single model family (LLaVA-v1.5-7B with LoRA) and appears to use single training runs; the headline aggregate gains are very small (100.18% vs 100.00% relative score), so no variance/seed reporting makes the 'matches full-scale VIT' claim statistically fragile.

The most impressive claims (83.3%/94.0% improvements at k≥4) rest on compositional-complexity labels of benchmark questions produced by Gemini-2.0-Flash — the same model used to generate the training data. This creates a potential annotation bias favoring COMPACT's data distribution, and the k≥4 subsets are likely small (the k=5 MM-Vet result of 20.0 vs 0.0 suggests very few samples); no confidence intervals or subset sizes are reported.

Gemini is used for both generation and verification, so quality control is circular: the verifier may share the generator's failure modes (hallucinated grounding, mislabeled capability requirements). A human evaluation of data quality is missing.

Some benchmark drops are obscured by the average: COMPACT underperforms the full 665K baseline on MME (1379.94 vs 1478.48) and CV-Bench (55.28 vs 60.92), which deserves more analysis given CV-Bench directly tests spatial/counting capabilities the recipe targets.

Possible stylistic confound: the generated answers are forced to be extremely concise (single word/short phrase), which may inflate scores on short-answer benchmarks (MM-Vet, MMStar) regardless of compositional ability; a control experiment isolating answer-style effects is absent.

Novelty is moderate: compositional instruction tuning, atomic-skill taxonomies, and data-efficient VIT recipes are all well-studied; the contribution is primarily a careful data-curation recipe rather than a new method or insight, and only one prior data-selection baseline (ICONS) is compared.
Reproducibility concerns from reliance on a closed, versioned model (Gemini-2.0-Flash), which the authors acknowledge; release of the dataset mitigates but does not eliminate this.

strengths: The core idea is reasonable and clearly motivated: explicitly balancing the compositional complexity (k) of visual instruction tuning data rather than relying on incidental composition in large datasets.
The paper is generally well organized, with a clear four-step data generation pipeline and prompts provided in the appendix, aiding reproducibility of the recipe.

A thoughtful set of ablations is included: unbalanced-k control (Table 3), leave-one-out capability analysis (Fig. 6), compositional complexity range (Fig. 7), and instruction-tuning data ratio (Fig. 8), which supports the claim that the balanced k-distribution is the main source of gains.
The authors honestly discuss limitations (closed-source generator bias, cost, vision-centric scope) and commit to releasing the generated data.
Using only 10% of the LLaVA-665K data budget while matching average relative performance is a practically relevant data-efficiency result if it holds.
weaknesses: The headline claims are overstated and potentially misleading. The abstract's '83.3% improvement on MMStar and 94.0% improvement on MM-Vet' are relative gains computed on tiny k>=4 question subsets (e.g., k=5 is 20.0 vs 0.0, almost certainly a handful of samples), not overall benchmark improvements. Actual overall gains on MM-Vet (+2.5 pts) and MMStar (+1.0 pt) are modest, and COMPACT clearly underperforms full VIT on MME (1379.9 vs 1478.5), CV-Bench (55.3 vs 60.9), and LLaVA-W (64.5 vs 68.5), contradicting 'comparable performance across all benchmarks'.

The central '100.18% vs 100.00%' relative-score claim of outperforming the full 665K dataset is a 0.18% margin with no variance reporting, no multiple seeds, and no statistical significance tests. Given noisy benchmark evaluations of MLLMs, this is not a defensible claim of superiority.

Only a single, dated backbone (LLaVA-v1.5-7B-LoRA) is evaluated. There is no evidence the recipe transfers to stronger or more modern MLLMs (e.g., LLaVA-Next, Cambrian, or a full fine-tuning setup), which weakens generality and significance.

The methodology has a circularity problem: Gemini-2.0-Flash both generates the compositional questions and verifies whether they require exactly k capabilities, and the same model is later used to annotate the k-complexity of evaluation benchmarks. There is no human verification of a sample, so the k-annotations for both training data and the headline k=4/k=5 analysis may be unreliable.

Limited novelty relative to prior work: capability-driven synthetic data generation with a frontier VLM, and 'atomic skill' decompositions, are well-trodden directions (e.g., the cited atomic-skills work [5], Mosaic-IT [20], and general synthetic VIT data recipes). The main contribution is a specific data-mixture design rather than a new technique or insight.

Baseline coverage is thin. Beyond Random and ICONS, no comparison against other strong data-efficient recipes (e.g., the data-selection works cited as [16, 26]) or against equal-budget augmentation baselines; 'outperforms full-scale VIT' rests on a single noisy aggregate.

Several ablation effects are very small and interpreted favorably: e.g., MMStar 34.53 vs 35.11 (0.6 pt) in Fig. 7 is presented as 'consistent improvements'. Without error bars, these differences are within noise.

Knowledge-intensive performance regresses substantially (OK-VQA 50.02 vs 57.96 for full VIT; MMMU gains are nil), showing the recipe trades breadth for compositionality, which softens the practical value of the data-efficiency claim.

Presentation issues undermine polish: inconsistent headline numbers between abstract and introduction (83.3%/94.0% vs 35.3->64.7), broken reference ('??' in Appendix C), duplicate bibliography entries ([22][23][24]), typos ('2. 08%', 'thepLLaVA-665K'), and a figure (Fig. 4) whose y-axis mixes accuracy with a data-distribution overlay in a way that is hard to parse.

Reproducibility concerns: the pipeline depends on a closed-source model whose behavior changes over time; the paper acknowledges cost but provides no estimate of generation cost or success rates, making it hard to assess practicality.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated core idea: explicitly controlling compositional complexity (k) of visual instruction tuning data, rather than treating compositionality as a byproduct of scale. The 'complexity cliff' analysis of LLaVA-665K (90% of questions require ≤2 capabilities) is a useful empirical contribution.
Strong data-efficiency results: COMPACT matches full LLaVA-665K VIT with ~10% of the data budget and clearly beats matched-size Random and ICONS baselines across 8 benchmarks.

Thorough ablation suite that supports the central claims: (1) unbalanced-COMPACT (matching LLaVA's skewed k-distribution) falls back to random-baseline performance, isolating balanced k-distribution as the key driver; (2) scaling compositional data from 2K-32K with matched VIT-only controls; (3) leave-one-out capability analysis; (4) k-range ablation; (5) VIT mixing-ratio ablation.

Interesting generalization finding: models trained only up to k=3 improve substantially on k=4 and k=5 benchmark questions (e.g., 64.7 vs 35.3 on MMStar k=4), suggesting genuine compositional generalization rather than mere exposure.

Transparent limitations section acknowledging closed-source generation costs, biases, and the vision-centric scope; the paper commits to releasing data. Reproducibility is aided by detailed prompts in the appendix.
Well-controlled experimental design: identical training configurations, image sets preserved from LLaVA-665K for fair comparison, and matched data budgets against baselines.
weaknesses: Limited model coverage: all experiments use only LLaVA-v1.5-7B-LoRA, an aging architecture, with 1 epoch and LoRA settings. There is no evidence the recipe transfers to stronger/modern MLLMs (e.g., Qwen2-VL, LLaVA-Next, InternVL), which weakens the claim of a general 'tuning recipe'.

Headline overall gains are thin: the aggregate relative score of 100.18% vs. the full 665K baseline is essentially at parity and likely within seed noise; no error bars, multiple seeds, or variance estimates are reported anywhere, despite substantial per-benchmark fluctuations. Claims of 'outperforming full VIT' rest on a 0.18% margin.

Potential circularity in evaluation: Gemini-2.0-Flash is used for data generation, data verification, and also for annotating the compositional complexity k of both training data and evaluation benchmarks. The k-dependent performance analysis (Fig. 4) and the k-averaged benchmark statistics could inherit systematic annotation bias from the same model that generated the training distribution.

Some per-benchmark results are actually worse than the full baseline (MME 1379.94 vs 1478.48; TextVQA 44.37 vs 46.99; LLaVA-W 64.5 vs 68.5), and the abstract/bullet framing (e.g., '83.3% improvement on MMStar') reports large relative gains on small k=4 subsets with tiny absolute counts, which risks overstating the contribution.

Novelty is moderate: compositional/atomic-skill decomposition for VLM data curation is an active area (Mosaic-IT, ConceptMix, atomic-skill decomposition at NeurIPS workshops), and the pipeline (capability sampling → LLM question generation → LLM self-verification → mixing) is a fairly standard synthetic-data recipe; the contribution is primarily empirical curation rather than a new method.

Only k up to 3 is used in training; reliability issues of Gemini at higher k are mentioned but not quantified, and the taxonomy of 10 atomic capabilities is heuristic (derived from literature) with no validation that it is complete or the right granularity.

Writing/polish issues: minor inconsistencies in reported numbers (e.g., MM-Vet gains stated as +8.6% in text vs table values; a stray '0.3577' for MMStar in §4.4), and Fig. 1's depiction of 'balanced' k is somewhat idealized relative to the actual generation process.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly articulated idea: treating sample complexity as a controllable metric (k-value) for VIT data curation, with a clean four-step data recipe that is easy to follow and reproduce.

Comprehensive evaluation: 8 multimodal benchmarks, comparison against strong data-reduction baselines (ICONS, D2-Pruning, SemDeDup, EL2N, Self-Filter, etc.) and the full LLaVA-665K recipe under matched data budgets (65K).

Thoughtful controls that strengthen causal claims: the complexity-matched COMPACT_llava experiment (Tab. 3) isolates the effect of k-value from generator/format effects, honestly showing roughly half of the gain comes from complexity; k-value range ablation (Fig. 4) and instruction-tuning-ratio ablation (Fig. 5) are informative.

Extensive supplementary analysis: per-capability ablation (Tab. 7), k-value breakdown on TextVQA and MMStar (Tabs. 4-6), failure mode and rejection-rate analysis (A.6), token-efficiency statistics (Tab. 8), and an open-source-generator replication with Qwen3-VL-4B (Tab. 9) that partially addresses closed-source dependence.
Transparent cost reporting (~2 hours, $86.5 API cost) and a commitment to release generated data, improving reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited scope of validation: all main experiments use only LLaVA-v1.5-7B with LoRA and a single seed; no second model family or scale is tested, so generality of the claim beyond this one setup is uncertain, and the headline 100.2% relative performance (a 0.2% margin over full data) is presented without error bars or significance testing.

Headline gains are modest and uneven: COMPACT matches full data on average but underperforms the full 665K baseline on several benchmarks (TextVQA 44.4 vs 47.0, CV-Bench 55.3 vs 60.9, LLaVA-W 64.5 vs 68.5, MME 1379.9 vs 1478.5); abstract framing ('outperforms the state-of-the-art method') leans on a narrow aggregate.

Circularity concerns in synthetic data: the same closed-source model (Gemini-2.0-Flash) generates questions, assigns k-values, verifies quality, and answers them, so the 'complexity' signal and the training targets share systematic biases; the k-value measure itself is LLM-assigned and validated only on TextVQA.

Novelty is incremental: compositional/capability-based data augmentation for VIT is closely related to prior work (Mosaic-IT, ConceptMix, Chae et al.'s atomic visual skills, Cambrian-style curation); the main contribution is applying capability composition to VIT data generation with a complexity knob rather than a fundamentally new technique.

Generated answers average only 1.7 tokens, producing very short supervision; the paper does not analyze the potential of distilling long-form reasoning, and knowledge-intensive results (A.3) show limited benefit, restricting the claimed scope to vision-centric skills.

Some internal inconsistencies and presentation issues: abstract claims MM-Star +2.9% over full data while Tab. 2 shows +1.0; the 5% VIT mixture complicates direct comparison with pure-subset baselines (partially addressed but not fully controlled at 65K scale).

strengths: The central research question—whether sample complexity, rather than sheer data volume, is the more informative axis for VIT data curation—is clearly articulated and well-motivated, and the exploratory experiment in Fig. 1 provides an intuitive starting point.

The evaluation is broad for this type of work: comparisons against the full LLaVA-665K baseline, a volume-matched random subset, and seven data reduction methods (including the relevant ICONS baseline) across eight benchmarks, all under identical training configurations.

The paper makes a genuine attempt to isolate the complexity effect via the COMPACT_llava distribution-matching control (Tab. 3) and includes ablations on k-value range, instruction-tuning ratio, atomic capability pruning (Tab. 7), token-level statistics, failure mode analysis, and an open-source generator (Qwen3) replication.
The appendix is thorough (system prompts, generation cost, data statistics), which supports reproducibility, and the authors commit to releasing the generated data.
weaknesses: Only about half of the claimed gain is actually attributable to the core idea: Tab. 3 shows that with the complexity distribution matched to LLaVA-665K (COMPACT_llava), performance is 97.55% vs. random 96.28%, and full COMPACT is 98.83%. This means roughly half the improvement over the random baseline comes from the generic synthetic regeneration pipeline itself rather than the k-value/complexity mechanism that the paper's title and framing emphasize. The central claim is therefore weaker than the abstract suggests.

The headline result of 100.2% relative performance is well within likely noise. There are no error bars, no multiple seeds, and no statistical significance tests, despite many differences between methods being under 1%. Claims of outperforming full-scale training rest on sub-point differences on individual benchmarks.

Evaluation is confined to a single model at a single scale (LLaVA-v1.5-7B with LoRA, one epoch). There is no evidence the recipe transfers to stronger base models, larger scales, or full fine-tuning, which limits the generality of the 'scalable recipe' claim.

Potential train–test image overlap is not addressed: COMPACT generates questions over images drawn from LLaVA-665K, and several evaluation benchmarks (e.g., TextVQA/InfoVQA images from OpenImages/Visual Genome, MMStar components) share image sources. Given that the method generates short, factual QA pairs over these same images, benchmark contamination is a serious concern that needs an explicit analysis.

The answers in COMPACT data average only 1.70 tokens (Tab. 8). This raises the question of whether gains on short-answer benchmarks reflect improved multi-capability visual reasoning or simply calibration toward short, single-word responses—an alternative explanation that is not ruled out.

Substantial circularity in methodology: the same model (Gemini-2.0-Flash) defines the capability taxonomy, assigns k-values, generates questions, and verifies quality. The k-value is thus a model-specific construct, and the claimed k-distribution analyses (Fig. 1, §4.3) inherit this bias; the acknowledged non-orthogonality and implicit object-recognition assumption further muddy the interpretation of k.

Novelty is moderate: combining synthetic question generation with data-efficient VIT is well-trodden territory (LLaVA-style regeneration, ICONS, Mosaic-IT, etc.), and the contribution is essentially a specific complexity-targeted prompting recipe rather than a new technique.
Despite token-efficiency framing (~47% fewer tokens), the training compute comparison with baselines is not reported, so the data-efficiency story is incomplete without a compute-matched control.

Knowledge-intensive results (OK-VQA, MMMU, MMMU-Pro in Fig. 9) show COMPACT trailing full training substantially (96.6% vs 100%), and the paper leans on the 'vision-centric' scoping to excuse this, which narrows the practical impact of the recipe.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated research question: the paper challenges 'quantity over quality' scaling in visual instruction tuning and proposes a concrete, testable alternative — increasing per-sample complexity by composing atomic visual capabilities.

The core method (COMPACT) is a practical four-step recipe (capability sampling, conversation generation, quality verification, dataset assembly) that is well described and includes useful engineering details such as iterative verification and diversity constraints.

Comprehensive evaluation: comparisons against the full LLaVA-665K baseline, a size-matched random subset, and seven data reduction/selection methods (EL2N, Perplexity, SemDeDup, D2-Pruning, Self-Sup, Self-Filter, ICONS) across eight multimodal benchmarks, with the headline claim (100.2% relative performance at 10% of the data budget) supported by the main table.

The paper takes confound control seriously. The COMPACT_llava experiment (Tab. 3), which matches the capability/k-value distribution to LLaVA-665K while controlling for the generator, helps isolate the effect of higher complexity rather than the data-generation procedure itself.

Useful ablations: k_gen range (Fig. 4), instruction-tuning data ratio (Fig. 5), per-capability ablations (Tab. 7), k-value-stratified MMStar analysis (Tab. 6), token-efficiency analysis (Tab. 8), and a replication with an open-source generator (Qwen3-VL-4B) that retains most gains (98.3% relative).

Transparent discussion of limitations, failure modes, and rejection statistics (A.6), plus a commitment to release the generated data; the reported generation cost (~$86.5, ~2 hours) supports reproducibility.
weaknesses: Circularity in complexity measurement: the same model family (Gemini-2.0-Flash) is used to generate questions, verify capability requirements, and later analyze the k-value distribution of both datasets. The claimed k-shift (mean 1.95 → 2.89) and capability-verification results may partly reflect the generator/verifier's own biases rather than intrinsic task complexity; no human annotation of k-values is provided to validate the metric.

The 10-capability taxonomy is acknowledged to be non-orthogonal and model-derived (object recognition is 'implicitly assumed' in most generations), which weakens the central claim that performance gains come from compositional complexity; Tab. 3 itself shows roughly half the gain comes from the generation procedure independent of k.

Per-benchmark results are uneven and somewhat undercut the headline: MME, TextVQA, CV-Bench, and LLaVA-in-the-Wild all drop below the full 665K baseline (e.g., CV-Bench 55.28 vs 60.92, LLaVA-W 64.50 vs 68.50). The 100.2% aggregate is an unweighted average that hides these regressions; long-form/open-ended performance (LLaVA-W) appears to suffer from the extremely short-answer style of the synthetic data (mean answer length 1.7 tokens).

Evaluation scope is narrow: all experiments use a single model (LLaVA-v1.5-7B-LoRA) with single training runs, no error bars or seeds, and no scaling to larger models or other architectures (e.g., Cambrian, Eagle), so generality of the recipe beyond one setup is unverified.

Novelty is moderate: compositional/capability-combination data generation has been explored in prior work (e.g., ConceptMix, Mosaic-IT, compositional instruction tuning, atomic-skills decomposition for evaluation), and the contribution is largely an application of these ideas to VIT data curation rather than a new technique.

Some exploratory claims are under-supported: the Fig. 1 'complexity improves performance' pilot has confounds (regeneration by Gemini itself changes style/quality), and answers distilled from Gemini's own perception may inject generator biases into ground-truth labels that cannot be fully removed by self-verification (as the authors admit in A.6).
